entry.title: Get three rechargeable wallet trackers that work with Find My for $69.97
entry.content:
Macworld

TL;DR: KeySmart SmartCard Gen 3 is a rechargeable wallet tracker that works with Apple Find My, and a 3-pack is on sale for $69.97 (reg. $119.97).

Most item trackers run on coin-cell batteries that eventually need replacing, and they’re usually too thick to sit flat in a wallet. If you’d rather carry something thinner that recharges, try a 3-pack of KeySmart SmartCard Gen 3 trackers. Three cards cost $69.97 (reg. $119.97), about $23 each.

Each card is 1.8mm thick, roughly two credit cards stacked together, so it slides into a card slot where an 8mm AirTag would bulge. Setup runs through Apple’s Find My app, and Precision Finding guides you straight to a wallet that’s somewhere in the room. If you walk away without it, your iPhone gets a separation alert.

Charging works on any standard Qi pad, and a full charge lasts up to 11 months. KeySmart says its Atlas Gen 3 chip connects 30% more reliably than standard trackers while using 30% less power. Every card is IPX8 waterproof, so a dunk in water or a spilled drink won’t damage it.

Android users can pair the same card with Google Find Hub instead, though each card works with one network at a time. With three in the box, you can keep one for your own wallet and give the other two to family, whichever phone they carry.

entry.title: Siri Recap Hands-On: Private, But Not Very Useful
entry.content:
With the watchOS 27.3 beta, Apple started testing Siri Recap. ‌Siri‌ Recap lets the Series 12 and Ultra 4 Apple Watch models listen to conversations to generate a brief summary of what was discussed. Actual audio is sectioned off from apps, Apple, and the rest of the OS, and then discarded after a summary is generated.


It's a privacy-forward way of tracking what's going on around you, but after two weeks of testing, it's clear that the privacy safeguards limit its usefulness. Overly brief summaries, lack of speaker labeling, and no original audio to compare against make ‌Siri‌ Recap unreliable.

Before I get into my experience, I want to make it clear that ‌Siri‌ Recap is a beta feature in beta software. It hasn't been released yet, Apple hasn't finished refining it, and it won't be available to the public until watchOS 27.3 launches in December. Still, the bones are in place. Some of the issues I encountered could improve before release, but others are the result of the way it's built.

My first recaps were from YouTube videos and Instagram Reels. ‌Siri‌ Recap can tell when I'm watching TV shows and movies, but it can't distinguish a YouTube video from a real-life conversation. I was surprised it summarized dialogue I wasn't involved in instead of waiting until it recognized my voice (which ‌Siri‌ can do). Listening in on ambient conversations makes it feel a little stalker-like. When ‌Siri‌ Recap is turned on, it's listening, and there's no indication for the people around you.


Most of my other recaps summarized short, inconsequential conversations with my partner that I don't need or want to revisit. I don't need to remember that my breakfast on Friday had one too many pieces of vegan bacon, or that my cat was playing with a silica packet. I don't need to remember discussions about Grand Theft Auto VI or that I saw a rabbit in the driveway the other day. There is an option to only have ‌Siri‌ Recap on at certain times of the day or in certain locations, which would eliminate that issue. Ironically, ‌Siri‌ did the best at summarizing shorter interactions I don't care about.


I've taken my cats to a few vet appointments recently, so I had an opportunity to test ‌Siri‌ Recap with genuinely important conversations where I get a flood of information. After the first visit, I learned ‌Siri‌ and I don't have the same opinion on the details that matter, and I found that summaries of longer conversations are just too concise and inaccurate to be helpful.

I told the vet my cat is picky and will only eat one kind of dry food, but stays hydrated because she drinks a lot of water. In a separate part of the conversation, I said she was gaining weight even though her prescription food isn't for kittens. ‌Siri‌ combined those two parts of the conversation into a summary that doesn't make sense, and I had that issue in almost every long conversation.

A few minutes later, I asked for a recommendation on heartworm medication because I've read about some problematic products that can make cats sick. The vet relayed a story about needing a particular brand for her cat because she has a rabbit at home, and rabbits are sensitive to a lot of medications. ‌Siri‌ Recap doesn't label speakers, so the summary of that conversation turned into a confusing amalgamation suggesting I have a rabbit at home. Inappropriately combining unrelated concepts is likely something that can be fixed, but the lack of speaker labels is intentional.


During a pre-surgery consultation, I think I ran into another limitation. Apple says potentially harmful content isn't summarized, which could cover a broad range of topics. Important parts of the conversation with the vet aren't in the summary, like some of the scarier surgical risks and resuscitation preferences. ‌Siri‌ doesn't say if anything was skipped because of the content, so I don't know if that information wasn't considered important or if it was filtered out.


Some of what ‌Siri‌ recapped was useful. If conversations were fact-heavy, ‌Siri‌ did a good job getting everything down, especially when dates were involved. I scheduled a follow-up appointment and ‌Siri‌ got the date right and the exact total of the bill when it was spoken aloud. Apple does say ‌Siri‌ Recap doesn't include financial info, so I'm not sure what counts. ‌Siri‌ is also surprisingly good at interpreting spoken medication names like benazepril and clopidogrel and correctly guessing what they're meant to be.


During a third vet visit, the recap did get many of the major points, but going over those notes made me realize this kind of summarization may not work, even when accurate. I had my own memory of the conversation and knew what I thought was important, but some of what ‌Siri‌ kept wasn't what mattered to me.

Those ‌Siri‌ details I re-read were cemented in my memory over other information when I revisited the conversation later in the week, subtly changing how I remember the appointment. I worry having notes that aren't my own will overwrite what I would have remembered without them. It's almost like having a picture of something that happened in my head, and then having someone tell me it happened differently.


‌Siri‌ Recap doesn't transcribe entire conversations for privacy reasons, but that leaves ‌Siri‌ to decide what's important enough to be written down in a discussion. I don't trust ‌Siri‌ to make that kind of decision, personally, and there's no option to check what ‌Siri‌ is leaving out since there are no raw files. I wouldn't want ‌Siri‌ Recap to record conversations in full because of the privacy concerns, but Apple's summarization alternative has shortcomings that affect its usefulness.

‌Siri‌ picks and chooses what matters, and in my two-week test, ‌Siri‌ merged concepts and conversations in ways that were more confusing than helpful over and over again. ‌Siri‌ Recap isn't a feature I'm going to use, and it's not a feature I'd recommend to others.

entry.title: MacRumors Giveaway: Win a 512GB OLED iPad Mini and a Year of Astropad Workbench
entry.content:
For this week's giveaway, we've teamed up with Astropad to offer MacRumors readers a chance to win a high-end 512GB OLED iPad mini with full A20 Pro chip and a free year of the Astropad Workbench software to go along with it.


Astropad Workbench is a remote desktop app and terminal built for using AI agents. It lets you control and monitor AI agents remotely, so it is a good fit for people who have a local AI setup or a service that gives an AI agent access to a Mac. Workbench supports everything from local LLMs to Claude Code, Codex, Xcode, and Cursor. With Workbench 1.4, the latest update, you can switch from the Terminal to the full desktop from the toolbar without needing to reconnect.

There are Astropad Workbench apps for Mac, iPad, and iPhone, so you can use your iPhone or ‌iPad‌ to interface with your Mac desktop and give commands to AI agents from wherever you are. Setup is simple, without the need for network configuration. Apps run natively on all supported devices, including the iPhone Duo.


You can even set Workbench up on a headless Mac mini with no display attached and access content from your iPhone or ‌iPad‌. Workbench also combines multiple Mac displays into one screen that matches the resolution of a remote device.


It's easy to check logs and output to verify agent work, restart failed tasks, and reconnect to long-running jobs. Multiple Macs are supported and you can switch between several machines connected to a single Workbench account. Intelligent sleep management makes sure your Mac is awake when you need it. Terminal sessions continue running after you disconnect, so you can start a session on one device like an ‌iPad‌ and then check in on it later from another device.

The app supports high-fidelity streaming for accurate colors and crisp text, an interactive mini-map for quick navigation, low latency, speech-to-text input, drag-and-drop file transfers, and on the ‌iPad‌, Apple Pencil support. There are no display recordings saved, and end-to-end AES–256 encryption is included. You can also veil your Mac's screen while a remote session is in progress so no one can see what you're doing.


Workbench is free for 20 minutes of daily access, with paid plans available at $14.99 per month or $79.99 per year. The app requires macOS 15 or later, iOS 26 or later, and iPadOS 26 or later. It works best with an Apple silicon Mac, though there is limited support for Intel Macs.

Macworld

Baseus Spacemate Docking Station 11-in-1

View Deal

There are tons and tons of docking stations you can buy out there, but so few of them can fix all of your Mac’s shortcomings. Well, this 11-in-1 Baseus Spacemate docking station is exactly what you need, and it’s down to $140 for Black Friday, a savings of 30 percent off its $200 MSRP.

The best thing about this dock is that it lets you add not one, not two, but three 4K monitors with both Macs and Windows laptops. DisplayLink technology bypasses the display limits built into most MacBooks, so you can run three 4K screens at once. That’s an incredible thing since many docking stations only support screen mirroring for Macs, and not full display extension.

The upright design with a magnetic base keeps your desk tidy, and a built-in LED screen shows what’s connected at a glance. A screen-lock button secures your computer with one tap when you step away.

While the extended screens are obviously amazing, there’s more to this docking station. The front of the device features USB-C and USB-A data ports so you can easily plug in flash drives without having to fiddle with the ports in the back. For the more permanent cables, you’ll find tons of ports on the back, including three HDMI ports, three USB-A ports, an audio jack, a 100W power-input port, and a Gigabit Ethernet port. That power input port can pass through 85W of power to your laptop so you won’t have to worry about using a different charger.

entry.title: The MacRumors Show: What's Next for iPhone Duo?
entry.content:
On this week's episode of The MacRumors Show, we discuss the iPhone Duo's new Face Unlock feature and all of the latest rumors about Apple's next-generation foldable iPhone.

Subscribe to The MacRumors Show YouTube channel for more videos

Apple this week added "Unlock with Front Camera" to the existing ‌iPhone Duo‌ in iOS 27.3 beta 2. The optional feature allows users to unlock the phone with facial recognition when it is closed, providing an alternative to the side-mounted Touch ID sensor. It does not offer Face ID's depth-sensing authentication, and ‌Touch ID‌ remains necessary for Apple Pay and accessing saved passwords.

The addition makes unlocking more convenient when fingerprint recognition is impractical, such as with wet hands, but introduces a distinction between unlocking the phone and authenticating sensitive actions. The same beta adds "Close to Lock," allowing users to lock the device when folding it shut instead of transferring their app to the outer display.


  • Hands-On With the iPhone Duo's New Face Unlock


‌Face ID‌ remains one of the biggest questions surrounding the next ‌iPhone Duo‌. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman says Apple has developed second-generation prototypes with ‌Face ID‌ beneath the outer display, but subsequently warned that the company is running out of time to finalize the feature. It could instead arrive with the third generation.

Meanwhile, the leaker known as "Digital Chat Station" claims current engineering units retain Touch ID, a 7.6-inch inner display, and a 5.4-inch outer display. ‌Face ID‌ limited to the outside would also leave a practical question about authentication when the phone is unfolded, potentially giving Apple a reason to retain fingerprint recognition alongside facial authentication.

The second-generation ‌iPhone Duo‌ is expected to launch in the fall of 2027. Its development reportedly received formal approval earlier this year, and Apple was already said to be testing it with iOS 28 in June.

Apple's longer-term goals reportedly include a thinner and lighter design, a dedicated telephoto camera, and Action button functionality. Gurman previously predicted that smaller components and computational processing could enable ‌Face ID‌ and a telephoto camera by the third generation.

Gurman says a third-generation model could arrive as early as 2028 with slightly larger inner and outer displays. He separately discussed a potential inner screen of around 7.9 to 8.1 inches for a future model, rather than a separate larger "Max" version. A bigger chassis could provide more room for additional hardware, but would also raise questions about added weight.

The leaker known as "Fixed Focus Digital" has linked improvements in the touchscreen MacBook Pro's hinge to work on the second- and third-generation ‌iPhone Duo‌. Reliability remains part of the discussion following reports of cracked displays on the current model.

For the controls, Apple could restore the missing Action button's functionality without adding another physical button. According to the leaker known as "Instant Digital," iPhones launching from the second half of 2027 could combine the controls, using a single press to open the camera and a long press for a customizable action.

Which iPad should you buy? With four different models, optional 5G cellular connectivity, multiple storage capacities, colors, and even refurbished options to consider, choosing the right iPad isn’t always straightforward.

Apple’s newest iPad is the iPad mini (A20 Pro), which went on sale November 6 with an 8.5-inch OLED display and a thinner, lighter design. The M4 iPad Air arrived in March 2026, and the M5 iPad Pro launched in October 2025. The standard iPad still uses the A16 chip from March 2025 and is the only iPad in Apple’s lineup without Apple Intelligence. Reports point to a replacement in the first half of 2027 that could add Apple Intelligence support.

This in-depth buying guide compares every iPad Apple currently sells and explains which model is best for different types of users. We’ll help you decide which offers the best value, how much storage you really need, which screen size is right for you, and whether it’s worth paying extra for a cellular model. We also look at whether new models are expected soon, so you can decide if now is the right time to buy. After our recommendations, you’ll find more detailed advice on displays, storage, processors, accessories, and Wi-Fi versus cellular.

The bad news is that Apple raised prices across the iPad range in June 2026, citing an unprecedented rise in component costs. In a statement, the company said it had “never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly” and explained that, while it had absorbed the extra costs for as long as possible, it had “reached a point where we need to begin raising prices on a number of products.” As a result, some iPads now cost hundreds of dollars more. We’ve updated all prices throughout this guide.

With prices in mind, if you are looking for a bargain, be sure to take a look at our roundup of the Best iPad Deals this Black Friday.

Best iPad to buy in 2026

If you mainly want an iPad for browsing, streaming, video calls, or the kids, the standard iPad (A16) is our budget pick. It starts at $449/£429 and has enough power for everyday apps and games.

If you want the smallest iPad, choose the iPad mini (A20 Pro). Its compact design is ideal for reading one-handed or playing games on the go. At $699/£699, it costs only $50/£50 less than the 11-inch iPad Air, so choose the Air if you’d get more use out of a bigger screen

If you need an iPad for work, study, or creative projects, the iPad Air offers the best balance of performance, features, and price. It supports Apple’s latest accessories, including the Apple Pencil and Magic Keyboard, making it the best choice for most buyers.

For professional users who edit photos and video, create artwork, play demanding games, or need the fastest performance and best display, the iPad Pro is the obvious choice.

Why we like it

The 13-inch iPad Pro gives you room to spread out in a tablet that’s thinner and lighter than the 13-inch iPad Air. Its tandem OLED display delivers deep blacks, bright HDR highlights, and smooth scrolling at up to 120Hz. The M5 chip and 12GB of memory in the base model give demanding creative apps plenty of room to run. Who it’s best for

This is the iPad for illustrators who want a large canvas, video editors who need room for a timeline, and anyone who regularly works across several apps. It’s also our top iPad pick for replacing a laptop, provided the iPad versions of your apps can handle the work you do. Factor in the cost of a Magic Keyboard or Apple Pencil Pro before you buy. If you mainly want a bigger screen, the 13-inch iPad Air is much better value.

Should you buy the 13-inch iPad Pro now?

Buy if you need the large OLED display and M5 performance now, especially if you find a substantial Black Friday discount. If your current iPad Pro still handles your work comfortably, we’d wait. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple is planning new 11-inch and 13-inch iPad Pro models for spring 2027, with faster chips and a similar design. Apple has also reportedly tested vapor-chamber cooling, which could help sustain performance during long exports or other demanding tasks. If you already own an M4 model, you already have the tandem OLED display, so there’s little reason to upgrade now.

iPad Buying Guide: What to look for when buying an iPad

As you can see from the above there are a lot of iPads sold by Apple—that doesn’t even include the many previous-generation iPads that are still on sale at various resellers and at Apple’s Refurbished Store (U.S) or U.K.

When confronted with so much choice what should you consider when deciding which iPad to buy?

For many the choice will be based on price and value for money. Some may be influenced by the screen size, others by the weight. The ability to get more than 512GB storage may be important, as may the inclusion of Face ID or Touch ID. Finally, the decision of whether to get a cellular version, which invites the assessment of the minefield of network contracts, will no doubt be a factor for some.

We will look at each of those factors below.

How iPad specs compare

The table below summarizes the main features of the iPads in Apple’s current lineup and highlights the price for each. We have more information about the individual iPads and buying advice below.

Which iPad is the best value for money?

One person’s value for money is another person’s extravagance.

You might be looking for the cheapest iPad. That would be the A16 iPad, launched in March 2025 and costing from $449/£429. It has a 10.9-inch screen, a 12MP rear-facing camera, an A16 chip, and 5G as an option. The main problem is that it doesn’t support Apple Intelligence, the bunch of AI features Apple has been shouting loudly about. With subsequent versions of iPadOS likely to lean heavily on Apple Intelligence you could get FOMO in the future if you buy this iPad. But if you only need a cheap iPad for the kids it’ll probably do the job, especially now that it has a reasonable amount of storage (no more struggling with 64GB).

An older iPad might be a better choice if you do want a bargain—especially if it is a model that supports AI (any M-series iPad Air will, for example). If you are happy to buy an older iPad model then there are plenty of discounts available while they are still in stock. There are also some great savings to be had on refurbished models – check out the Apple Refurbished Store and other places to buy a refurbished iPad. We also recommend you check our best iPad deals round up.

If you have more to spend, what can you get for your money? The A20 Pro iPad mini justifies its price tag of $699/£699 with its faster (Apple Intelligence-capable) A20 Pro processor, True Tone flash, and a fully laminated, better-quality display, among other things. But its biggest draw will probably be its size for those who want a small iPad. The iPad mini is not much bigger than a hard-backed book making it the perfect size to carry around in a bag and a great size for kids. That’s assuming you want a small iPad—if not, then it won’t be for you.

Next up is the M4 iPad Air, which now starts at $749/£749 for the 11-inch model. It might be worth every extra penny if you want a faster M4 processor. The iPad Air display is still superior to that of the standard iPad, fully laminated and with an antireflective coating (like the iPad mini).

The introduction of an 13-inch iPad Air means that you no longer need to fork out extra for the iPad Pro if you want a larger display on your iPad.

The M5 iPad Pro, last updated in October 2025, is the ultimate in this category. Now starting at $1,199/£1,199, the Pro has a lot to offer, with an incredible display and an M5 chip for starters. But we think these features are probably more than the average person needs. Then again, if you need those features you can’t beat it, unless you want a bigger screen, in which case get the 13-inch iPad Pro.

Those are the prices that Apple sells its iPads for, but you don’t have to pay that much. Take a look at our regularly updated iPad deals page for the lowest prices and best discounts on iPads new and old.

iPad screen size: Which size iPad to choose

Size is a question of taste rather than simply going for the biggest iPad you can get your hands on. Bigger isn’t necessarily better if what you need is small and light.

The most obvious aspect of this decision comes down to screen size. All screens are measured diagonally from corner to corner, or from the place where the corners would be. You’ve got four options:

  • 8.3-inch iPad mini
  • 10.9-inch iPad
  • 11-inch iPad Air and iPad Pro
  • 13-inch iPad Air and iPad Pro

But how big a screen do you really need? You can think of the tablets in terms of print publications: the mini is roughly the height and width of a paperback book; the mid-size iPads are closer to a hardback (albeit much slimmer); and the 13-inch iPad Pro and iPad Air are like a magazine (remember them?)

The screen on the 13-inch iPad Pro is a tiny bit bigger than that on the 13-inch iPad Air, that’s 2,752 x 2,064 pixels vs 2,732 x 2,048 pixels.

The larger screen is obviously better for immersive entertainment. Whether watching films or playing games, it’s a more enjoyable, richer experience. But really this is a question of priorities. Are you more set on getting maximum screen space, or are you willing to compromise on that front in order to get a lower price tag and improved portability?

  • iPad Pro 13-inch (2025): 281.6mm x 215.5mm x 5.1mm; 579g/582g (Wi-Fi/cellular)
  • iPad Pro 11-inch (2025): 249.7mm x 177.5mm x 5.3mm; 444g/446g
  • iPad Air 13-inch (2026): 280.6mm x 214.9mm x 6.1mm 616g/617g
  • iPad Air 11-inch (2026): 247.6mm x 178.5mm x 6.1mm; 464g/465g
  • iPad A16 (2025): 248.6mm x 179.5mm x 7mm; 477g/481g
  • iPad mini 8.3-inch (2024): 195.4mm x 134.8mm x 6.3mm; 293g/297g

Want the lightest iPad? As you’d expect, the iPad mini is a lot lighter than the other iPads. There’s a big gap between that device and even the mid-size iPads. As well as its markedly lower weight the mini also has a smaller body, which slips easily into a rucksack or jacket pocket. If you plan to mainly use your iPad out and about, on vacation, or commuting, or perhaps you’re buying an iPad for a child, the mini is your best bet.

The iPad, 11-inch iPad Air, and 11-inch Pro are pleasingly portable, but they still can’t match the mini for portability. The iPad has a similar length and width to the Air, but is thicker and heavier; the Pros are slimmer still.

The 13-inch Pro and Air are considerably less portable than their smaller cousins, but we think Apple has done well to keep the weight down, especially with the Pro, which is actually thinner than the iPad Air (go figure): it remains a slender, relatively lightweight, and portable alternative to a laptop.

How much storage do iPads need?

iPads in the current lineup offer anywhere from 128GB to 2TB of storage, but if you are looking at an old, refurbished, or preowned iPad you could be confronted with 64GB or even 32GB storage, which isn’t enough. But what storage capacity do you really need for an iPad?

Well, first of all, remember that you can’t upgrade the storage of an iPad at a later date: this is your limit from now until you buy another iPad, so aim high and buy as much storage as you can afford. It’s better to spend an extra few pounds now than to buy an entire new iPad in six months.

Storage capacity is mainly used up by three things: music, photos, and videos. If you want to keep lots of films or TV shows–or even a few, to be honest–then you need high storage: probably 256GB or higher for video fans. If you’re buying an iPad with the kids in mind, remember that you’ll want storage space for multiple episodes of their favorite show on a long car journey.

The same applies if you have large photo or music libraries, although iCloud Photos and iTunes Match make it possible to keep your stuff in the cloud and access it remotely. The problem with iCloud Photos is that it will store low-res versions of all your images, from all your devices, on your iPad. If your library is huge then even these low-res versions of images can take up a lot of space on your iPad. If you don’t have a lot of storage on your iPad then avoid using iCloud Photos.

The other thing that will fill up your storage is apps, especially games which will use up a lot of space. For that reason gamers should aim high on storage: The iPad, iPad Air and iPad mini start with 128GB and the Pro begins at 256GB. We recommend getting what you can afford. See: How much storage do you need on an iPhone or iPad? for more advice.

Should you get the most powerful iPad?

The iPad Pro models are, as you would expect, faster than their smaller and cheaper equivalents, next up is the Air, then the iPad mini and finally the iPad. You can get an idea of relative speed by looking at a few relevant specs:

  • iPad Pro 13-inch (2025): M5; 12GB/16GB RAM
  • iPad Pro 11-inch (2025): M5; 12GB/16GB RAM
  • 13-inch iPad Air (2026): M4; 12GB RAM
  • 11-inch iPad Air (2026): M4; 12GB RAM
  • iPad mini (2024): A17 Pro; 8GB RAM
  • iPad 10.9-inch (2025): A16; 6GB RAM

The M-series chips have won widespread acclaim in the Mac range and produce outstanding performance in the iPads. But that doesn’t mean the A chips are sub-standard or incapable of running modern apps; keep in mind that much of the software on the App Store was designed with A chips in mind, and even now most developers will want to make their software accessible for as many iPad owners as possible.

Stage Manager lets you group and arrange app windows on the iPad’s own screen, including on the A16 iPad and A20 Pro iPad mini. If you want to move app windows between your iPad and an external monitor, look for extended display support. You’ll get it on the M-series iPad Air and iPad Pro, as well as on the A20 Pro iPad mini with iPadOS 27.2 or later

How powerful you need your iPad to be will be based on your requirements (and how long you intend to use your iPad for). The most demanding graphic-design, video-editing, and audio apps will see better performance on the M5, M4, M3 and even M2 processor, so if you’re looking at high-level workloads multiple years down the line the M5 and M4 would be a better option.

Another important factor to consider is memory. Apple doesn’t advertise the fact, but the iPad has only 6GB. The mini has 8GB and Air gets a jump up to 12GB, while the Pros have either 12GB or a whopping 16GB of RAM, depending on your storage tier: the 1TB and 2TB versions get the higher RAM allocation.

If you want to run Apple Intelligence, you must have an iPad with at least 8GB of RAM. With the current iPad lineup, Apple Intelligence can run on all iPads expect the iPad. Learn more about Apple Intelligence.

Overall, we would advise those who want to use highly demanding apps, such as video and image editors and graphically advanced games, to choose an iPad Pro or Air. If you’re going to be using your tablet for the odd bit of email and web surfing, you’ll find an iPad or iPad mini perfectly decent.

Should you get a Cellular iPad?

For most people cellular connectivity is a luxury, even if it’s a nice one to have. For an extra $200/£200 or $150/£150 depending on the iPad, you’ll be able to access the web and email, and use connected apps, away from a Wi-Fi network. You also need to factor in the cost of a data plan and find a network provider.

Consider carefully how often you’re going to do that: with an iPad mini there’s likely to be more on-the-go use than with a full-size iPad, but it’s still a lot to pay for something you may only use from time to time. Have you got a regular (overground) commute where you’d enjoy catching up on news headlines or e-mail? Then it could be worth the extra.

We think the best option, if you want to be able to get data on your iPad when you are out and about, is to create a hotspot and share it from your iPhone. Then you can use your iPad as if it is on the cellular network. Read about how to create an iPhone hotspot to share your mobile web connection to your iPad.

Just bear in mind that the cellular option also brings with it a GPS radio, meaning you’ll be able to input accurate location data when using your device on the go.

The other concern when buying a cellular iPad is whether to buy your iPad on a contract. Network providers will allow you to pay for your iPad and the data contract over a number of months—but after that term is up, and certainly not before, you may not be able to switch to a different data provider. Buying on contract may also mean that the iPad is locked to the original contract provider—which can also be a problem if you want to sell it in the future. Here’s how to unlock an iPad from its network, once you’ve fulfilled your contractual obligations.

Should you buy a refurbished iPad?

Apple

We’ll mention this only briefly because it’s covered in detail here: Why a refurbished iPad could be the best tablet for you, but one option you should absolutely consider is Apple’s Refurbished Store U.S or U.K. It’s a sort of halfway house between new and second-hand: the devices are generally ones that have been returned within the 28-day period in which you are legally allowed to change your mind about a purchase, or they have been returned due to a fault that has been rectified, or they were ex-display or ex-demo units from Apple’s stores or marketing. You can rest assured that Apple has checked all the refurbished iPads that it sells thoroughly, replaced any problematic components, and rated them as good as new (and you get a full one-year warranty to prove it).

Apple’s not the only place to buy a refurbished iPad, so beware that all refurbished iPads are not the same, so do check the small print before you buy. Look for refurbished models that have been fully checked out by Apple-certified engineers, especially those that come with a guarantee.

Our best advice is to only consider the current or previous generation iPads when looking at refurbished models, then you are less likely to be caught out by a sub-par tablet.

Buying a refurbished iPad from a reputable company is definitely preferable to buying a used iPad from someone on eBay. It’s too often the case that secondhand iPads sold that way end up as useless bricks because the person selling it didn’t properly log out of their account.

Another way to save money is to buy from a reseller who is selling discontinued stock at a discount. We often see resellers significantly dropping the price on older iPad models that are usually just one generation out of date—just beware, they sell out quick!

Should you buy the newest iPad generation?

Speaking of older iPads, even if functioning perfectly right now, older models will reach the end of their useful life sooner than the newest models and that is a good reason to avoid buying an iPad that is more than one or two generations old. But keep in mind that iPads tend to start slowing down at around two to three years of age; at the four- or five-year mark you should expect noticeable loss of performance and you won’t be able to get all the latest software updates. The current iPad range launched in 2024 and 2026, the most recent being the iPad Air in March 2026 and the oldest being the iPad mini in October 2024.

Another reason to buy a recent iPad is the operating system it runs. Apple only supports recent versions of iPadOS with security updates, so that could mean that only iPadOS 26 and iPad OS 18 get security updates, although Apple has been known to update older iPadOS versions when necessary. See How long does Apple support iPads? for more information.

So, while you don’t have to buy the newest generation, we would recommend that you buy one that was launched relatively recently to be sure that Apple will support it for as long as you intend to own it. On that basis, any of the iPads listed above should be a safe bet because they support the iPadOS that Apple will support for the next three years, and for many the support will stretch on for more years.

Buying advice: Which iPad should you buy?

The standard iPad is a good option for newcomers and those who will mostly use their iPad as a media consumption device with some light work. The one key thing it still lacks, despite a 2025 update, is support for Apple Intelligence.

For most people, our recommendation is the iPad Air (2026). The update in March 2026 brought it an M4 processor, which is more than enough for an iPad right now, but even 2024’s M2 iPad Air will be more than sufficient if you find one on sale.

Mind you, the iPad Air is still expensive compared to the standard iPad and the iPad mini, and to most rival tablets out there. But, the addition of the 13-inch model means that if you want a big screen you don’t have to fork out for the iPad Pro.

The iPad mini is mainly recommended for those who see portability as their main priority. It’s an excellent little device, although the smaller screen makes it less immersive for games and entertainment options.

The remaining iPads will be too expensive for the average buyer – especially now that Apple has hiked up prices. The 11-inch and 13-inch Pro models are amazingly powerful and well-made, and the M5 is excellent, but probably more power than anyone really needs right now. But if you’re a creative professional, the Pro is the iPad to get.

Finally, before taking the plunge, have you considered if a laptop might suit your needs better? See iPad vs MacBook for more advice on that front.

If you’re thinking of buying an iPad for college or university you might also like to read our guide to the best iPad for students. You may also like to read our best iPad for kids guide. We also have a Best iPad for Seniors guide.

entry.title: Microsoft to Retire 'To Do' Apps Next Year
entry.content:
Microsoft will retire its "To Do" apps on June 30, 2027, ending support for its task manager on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, Android, and the web.


In its retirement announcement, Microsoft directs work and school account users to Planner. Personal Microsoft accounts cannot access Planner, including those with Microsoft 365 Personal or Family subscriptions, leaving those users to find another task management app entirely.

Switching to Planner will not transfer users' existing To Do tasks and lists. Those tasks will remain available within Planner until June 30, 2027, but users will lose access to them there after that date. Microsoft plans to provide an export option before To Do retires, although it has not explained what the export will include or whether other apps will be able to import it.

Mac users moving to Planner will also lose the option of a dedicated desktop app. Planner is available through a browser or Microsoft Teams, and Microsoft has no plans to release a native Mac or Windows app to replace To Do. Neither option offers the same ability to manage tasks offline as the existing desktop apps.

To Do grew out of "Wunderlist," the popular task manager whose developer, 6Wunderkinder, Microsoft acquired in 2015. Wunderlist's appeal at the time was its combination of simplicity, shared lists, and synced support across platforms. Microsoft introduced To Do in April 2017 as Wunderlist's intended successor, built by the same team.

Initially available as a preview for iPhone, Android, Windows, and the web, it added a My Day view that suggested tasks to focus on. Microsoft said it would keep Wunderlist running until its key features were available in the new app. A native Mac app followed in June 2019, bringing offline access, shared lists, flagged Outlook emails, and a compact window for viewing tasks alongside other apps.

Wunderlist was discontinued in May 2020, completing the earlier transition to To Do. Microsoft now plans to begin rolling out an updated My tasks experience in Planner in December 2026.

entry.title: First legitimate iPhone Air 2 dummy unit shows off key upgrade to spur sales
entry.content:
Macworld

While everyone scrambles to find an iPhone Duo before January, those who choose to wait until 2027 to upgrade their iPhone may be in for a treat. For the first time, Apple will hold a second iPhone launch in the spring for the models that are still part of the iPhone 17 crop and one model is looking to get a huge upgrade.

In the spring, Apple is expected to release the iPhone 18 and 18e, as well as the iPhone Air 2. While we’re not expecting huge changes with either the iPhone 18 or 18e, the iPhone Air 2 has been rumored to get two key upgrades that held it back from being a sales success. And now it looks like we have proof of one of them.

Well-known and highly accurate leaker Sonny Dickson has posted images of the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 dummy units that are used by case and accessory makers. While the overall design remains the same, we can clearly see a plateau at the top of the Air with holes for two cameras, matching the iPhone 18. We’ve heard for a while that Apple is planning to add a second ultra-wide camera to the Air 2, and this image seemingly confirms it.

Otherwise, the phones appear identical to their current counterparts, with the Air sporting a slightly larger display than the 18 (6.5 inches versus 6.3 inches) and both featuring the larger Dynamic Island. The iPhone 18 sill has the same vertical camera array in the left corner rather than the horizontal plateau of the Air. In addition to the extra camera, the iPhone Air 2 is also expected to gain a larger battery and a slightly thinner body.

Of note, Dickson calls this phone the iPhone 18 Air, which would be a name change. Even though the Air debuted as part of the iPhone 17 lineup, Apple opted to leave “17” off the name like the iPhone Duo. A name change would suggest that Apple plans on keeping the Air as part of the iPhone lineup and will upgrade it on an annual basis.

By all accounts, the iPhone Air was a sales flop, with users opting for the models with more cameras and bigger batteries over the Air’s unique ultra-thin design. However, Apple is looking to upgrade the follow-up model that addresses its two biggest complaints. The only other issue is the price. Apple bumped the starting price to $1,099 in September, which might be a little too high for a non-Pro phone that doesn’t fold. Here’s hoping it dips under $1,000 again in the spring.

What is it? A power bank designed to perfectly fit the Apple iPhone Duo.

Who is it best for? iPhone Duo owners in need of portable recharging.

Who should skip it? Owners of standard non-folding iPhones.

We’ve reviewed the best magnetic wireless power banks for iPhone and all work with every iPhone since the iPhone 12, with the exception of older iPhone mini models and the odd iPhone 16e that lacks MagSafe altogether. Their compatibility stems from the iPhone retaining its basic shape and magnetic coil arrangement through each series.

The newer iPhone Duo, however, takes a different shape due to its folding nature and unique dimensions. Standard power banks will clamp onto the iPhone Duo but are likely to hang off the bottom of the phone, reducing stability and charging efficiency.

Baseus has therefore designed its latest portable charger, the PicoGo AM72, especially for the iPhone Duo.

How does the PicoGo AM72 fit the iPhone Duo?

Folded, Apple’s iPhone Duo measures 4.64 inches in height, 3.31 inches wide, and 0.44 inches deep (118 x 84 x 11.3mm).

The Baseus PicoGo AM72 measures up as 3.36 x 3.19 x 0.31 inches (85 x 81 x 7.9mm), and weighs in at 4.2oz (119g). It’s a close match in width to the Duo (but wider than a standard iPhone) and nestles at the end of the iPhone without spilling over. Rounded corners make it an appealing fit.

Foundry / David Price

When magnetically fixed to the Duo, there’s no overhang that you’d find if attaching just about any other power bank. This means the two together will slip into your pocket without impacting the wireless charging. The magnetic connection feels strong and secure.

The AM72’s body has an aluminum alloy body, and is available in Silver for the Star White Duo and (from December) Blue for Night Sky.

Simon Jary

How does the PicoGo AM72 perform as a portable charger?

The PicoGo AM72 supports up to 15W Qi2 wireless charging and up to 25W wired charging with the included USB-C cable. The power bank itself recharges at up to 18W over USB-C. To be fair, we haven’t seen a 25W 5K power bank yet, only 10K.

Baseus

The difference in power/speed is around 15 minutes when charging the iPhone Duo from 0-50%: 30 minutes (25W) vs 45 minutes (15W).

Magnetic wireless charging is not yet as powerful—and therefore fast—as wired charging, and so Baseus includes a short USB-C charging cable that does support 25W for when you’re in a hurry. Input power (the speed at which the power bank is recharged itself) is 18W.

Baseus

In terms of battery capacity, the PicoGo AM72 is a 5000mAh (milliamp hours) power bank (aka 5K) but more accurately 19.55Wh (watt hours), which is a little over the average for 5K portable chargers.

We test power banks by running the iPhone’s battery down to 0% and then wirelessly connecting the portable charger to run until it is empty itself. In our wireless recharge test, the PicoGo AM72 took the iPhone Duo from 0% to 60%. The 5K power banks we’ve tested on non-folding iPhones averaged 76%, though the different test phones make a direct comparison difficult. (Battery testing by Macworld’s David Price.)

A 60% recharge from a power bank as slim and short as this one is impressive and should get you to your next static charging point.

Foundry / David Price

Baseus claims that the AM72’s graphene and aerogel insulation layers aid heat dissipation—with its surface temperature staying below 100°F (38°C), which cooler than the industry standard of 118.4°F (48°C). In hand, the power bank did feel a little warm during peak charging, but this is common with powerful wireless chargers.

Thanks to NFC, you can tap your iPhone against the power bank to check battery health and charging status in the Baseus app. Tap again to refresh the charging reading.

Baseus

How much does the Baseus PicoGo AM72 cost?

Available at the time of writing in the U.S. only, the Baseus PicoGo AM72 is priced at $79.99. The darker model will be released in December.

The BMX SolidSafe Duo 5K is another power bank designed for the iPhone Duo, and we’ll be testing this portable charger soon; it’s also priced at $79.99.

Should you buy the Baseus PicoGo AM72 power bank for iPhone Duo

iPhone Duo owners will appreciate this magnetic wireless power bank that’s designed to perfectly fit their folding phone. It’s slim yet attaches strongly to the phone and performed well in our recharge tests. Faster charging is possible with the included USB-C cable.

entry.title: Apple job listing gives away proactive agentic AI project (Update: Pulled)
entry.content:
Macworld

Update November 20: Apple has pulled the job listing.

A new job listing for a Senior Engineering Manager at Apple’s Cupertino campus has given away an open secret: Apple is working on an autonomous, proactive AI agent. That link above goes to a broken page becuase the jjob listing has since been pulled, but we can learn a bit about Apple’s future plans from its description:

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the listing begins. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”

AI agents that operate continuously and proactively in the background are the latest hot item, and some think are the next big frontier in consumer AI. It’s the natural successor to chatbots, and is often perceived as the big step that will get the whole world hooked on AI.

Currently, AI agents are extremely popular in the App Store. Meta’s Muse is the #2 free app, behind only TikTok. Chatbots that have added agentic capabilities hold other top spots: ChatGPT is #3, Claude is #5, and Gemini is #7.

Each of these has varying degrees of autonomy, and many of the Mac apps from these companies can access your Mac’s data and operate its app. Google’s Gemini Mac app was just updated to be able to use your Mac for you, for example.

Apple’s job posting makes it clear that the company is building its own similar product. The job description is as follows:

People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service. We’re building AI agents that can do the same. We’re a team of engineers, AI applied researchers, and systems specialists working on general-purpose computer-use agents. These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.

As a senior leader in this org, you will own the technical direction and delivery of our agent platform and the AI capabilities built on it. You will lead and develop a team of managers and engineers. You will also build the AI and systems talent that will define what we can ship next. You’ll work closely with partner teams across Siri, UI frameworks, and AFM and more. Your job is to turn their capabilities, and ours, into agents that are capable, reliable, and safe.

The posted job listing is for a senior management position, someone who will, “Set the technical vision, roadmap, and quality bar for AI agents that work across apps, browsers, terminals, code, and APIs.” If that is the case, and Apple is trying to assemble its team and direct the vision for the project now, then it is at least a year behind its competitors. Competing services have proactive and autonomous AI agents available to consumers today–even if Apple races ahead at top speed, it’s hard to imagine a similar product reaching users until at least the fall of 2027, by which time Meta, OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic will be on their second or third generation of consumer AI agents.

entry.title: First Look at iPhone Air 2 and iPhone 18 Revealed By Dummy Models
entry.content:
New images of dummy models offer an early look at the purported designs of the iPhone Air 2 and iPhone 18, showing a new dual rear camera arrangement for the Air and a largely unchanged appearance for the standard model.


In a new post on X, leaker Sonny Dickson highlights the ‌iPhone Air‌'s move from one rear camera to two as the biggest change. The standard ‌iPhone 18‌, he says, retains a design similar to the iPhone 17. A second image shows the fronts of the mockups.

The ‌iPhone Air‌ 2 mockup places both lenses horizontally toward the left side of its raised camera plateau, with the microphone and flash to their right. The plateau continues to stretch across most of the device's width. By comparison, the standard ‌iPhone 18‌ dummy has two vertically stacked lenses within a smaller, pill-shaped camera bump.

First look at the iPhone 18 Air and iPhone 18 dummy units. The biggest change is the iPhone 18 Air, which now features two rear cameras instead of one, while the standard iPhone 18 retains a design similar to the iPhone 17. pic.twitter.com/MdOVuwPlm3

— Sonny Dickson (@SonnyDickson) November 20, 2026



Dummy models are nonfunctional replicas typically produced using leaked dimensions and design information from Apple's supply chain. Accessory manufacturers use them to develop and test cases before the actual devices are available, allowing products to be ready around launch. This preparation makes dummy models a recurring source of early design previews, particularly for camera layouts, button placement, and overall proportions.

The second rear camera has been a consistent ‌iPhone Air‌ 2 rumor for more than a year. The Information reported in November 2025 that Apple was considering the addition as part of a redesign, with subsequent reports continuing to point to a dual-camera system.

The first-generation ‌iPhone Air‌ has a single 48-megapixel Fusion camera. Analyst Jeff Pu later predicted that its successor would gain a 48-megapixel Ultra Wide camera, adding a wider field of view to the device's photography capabilities.

Beyond the additional camera, Pu expects the next ‌iPhone Air‌ to feature an A20 Pro chip, a slightly smaller Dynamic Island, Apple's C2 modem, and an N2 wireless networking chip, while retaining a 6.5-inch display and 12GB of RAM. The Information previously reported that Apple was working on a larger battery, reduced weight, and vapor chamber cooling for the second-generation model.

The standard ‌iPhone 18‌ is expected to adopt the A20 chip and C2 modem, and could also gain a smaller ‌Dynamic Island‌ like the iPhone 18 Pro. Ming-Chi Kuo expects 9GB of memory, up from the ‌iPhone 17‌'s 8GB, while Pu predicts 12GB.

Both devices are expected to launch around March 2027, alongside the iPhone 18e.

What is it? The slimmest magnetic wireless power bank we’ve tested.

Who is it best for? iPhone owners who desire the most portable charger.

Who should skip it? People who want a power bank with a higher capacity and charging speed.

Like most things, except the average human being, devices are forever getting slimmer and lighter. Apple’s iPhone Air took thinness to a new level, with the phone measuring only 0.22 inches (5.64mm) at the waist.

Putting the Air in a case seems perverse, but clamping a power bank on its skinny body is sometimes going to be a necessity—especially given that its own internal battery is smaller than other iPhones (3,149mAh vs 3,692mAh for the iPhone 17 released at the same time) in order to make it so damn flat.

Power banks have been getting into the slimming act too. Recently the BMX SolidSafe Air 5K and Baseus Picogo Air AM71 Magnetic Power Bank drew in a dead-skinny heat at a depth of just 0.27 inches (6.8mm).

Momax

Just how thin is the Momax 1-Power S.Pass Air power bank?

At just 6.3mm thick, the Momax 1-Power S.Pass Air takes the crown as the thinnest magnetic power bank we’ve tested. Momax lists it at 6.0mm, with a tolerance of ±0.2mm, and our digital caliper put our sample at 6.3mm. That extra 0.3mm is an extremely slender margin that few will notice.

Looking at it, it’s difficult to imagine a power bank getting any thinner due to the USB-C port nearly touching the edges. But Apple managed to get the Air down to 0.22 inches (5.64mm) so it must be possible. The only other thing holding back skinnier power banks is the battery inside, and any included safety and cooling techs.

While it carries the label ‘5K’ for 5000mAh (milliamp hours), a more accurate measure is in watt hours, and the Momax battery itself is rated at 19.25Wh—over the average 19Wh for a 5K portable charger.

Simon Jary

How does the Momax 1-Power S.Pass Air power bank perform?

We test every portable charger in the same way: run an iPhone down to 0% and then connect the power bank. We do it up to three times and publish the best result. A 5K power bank will run dry itself before the iPhone has reached 100%—the average Macworld Recharge Score is 76%, with the highest we’ve tested reaching 90% (Ugreen MagFlow Air).

The Momax 1-Power S.Pass Air scored 73%, a little below average. While not at the top of the recharge scores, it promises to take your depleted iPhone back to nearly three-quarters of power while staying super slim in your pocket or handbag.

Its slimness might explain the lower recharge score as power banks lose efficiency when hot, and possible the slim profile increases this and other wireless factors.

It’s a Qi2 wireless charger, so maxes at 15W power output. Look to a 10K power bank for 25W and up to 200% recharge scores, but of course you’ll not get anything as slim as the S.Pass Air 5K.

You’ll get a faster charge if you use the power bank’s USB-C port with a cable to connect your iPhone, as that outputs at up to 22.5W.

Momax also sells a larger model, the 1-Power S.Pass 10000mAh Semi-Solid-State Magnetic Battery Pack. This has advantages such as 25W wireless charging (30W wired) and a larger battery capacity (38.8Wh) as well as utilizing the more durable semi-solid-state battery technology. On the downside, it’s over twice as deep as the 5K, at 0.57 inches (14.5mm) and 208g in weight. Check out all the 10K magnetic power banks we’ve tested in our roundup of the best wireless portable chargers.

Momax

Does the S.Pass Air look good?

It’s difficult to take a decent photo of this stainless-steel portable charger as it has a glossy, almost mirrored front. It will work as a mirror in decent lighting conditions, albeit one with a strong tint if you pick the Dusky Cherry color.

Turn it on its side and you’ll barely notice it, but it looks gorgeous front on, although I do worry it might attract scratches if left tumbling around in a bag or frequently drawn from a rough trouser pocket.

It’s available in Dusky Cherry – perfect for the latest Burgundy iPhone 18 Pro – as well as Silver and Titanium.

Our sample weighed 111g, well below the 129g average for a 5K portable charger. Only the Baseus PicoGo Air AM71 at 105g is lighter. You won’t notice the extra 6g.

How much does the 5K S.Pass Air cost?

The Momax 1-Power S.Pass Air 5000mAh Slim Magnetic Power Bank costs $64.99 direct from Momax. At the time of writing, it’s not available via Amazon or other retailers, so you’ll need to add $15 shipping (U.K. $25). Free shipping is available on orders of USD $99 or more to the U.S. and U.K. so you could add a second battery pack or another Momax product to save on shipping.

If you can bear the extra 0.5mm depth, the Baseus Picogo Air AM71 costs $69.99 / £79.99, with the semi-solid-state BMX SolidSafe Air a little cheaper at $59.99 / £59.99. Both are also available in iPhone-matching burgundy as well as other colors.

Is the Momax 1-Power S.Pass Air worth buying?

If you want the leanest power bank available today, the Momax 1-Power S.Pass Air is the real skinny. It looks great, will get lost in a pocket, and takes your iPhone to nearly 75% from 0% when you need it most.

entry.title: WhatsApp Raises Group Chat Limit to 1,500 Members
entry.content:
WhatsApp is allowing group chats to have up to 1,500 members on iPhone and Android, up from the previous limit of 1,024 participants, according to WABetaInfo.


The increase means group chat admins have room for another 476 people in a single conversation. The jump should make it easier for schools, clubs, and other large organizations to communicate with their members, rather than having to split them across separate chats.

There's no setting to enable the new higher limit, as existing groups will gain the extra capacity automatically as the change reaches their accounts. The higher limit also applies to individual group chats within WhatsApp Communities, which bring related groups together under a shared hub.

WhatsApp has yet to officially announced the change, and its Help Center still lists the maximum group size as 1,024 members. Even so, the rollout is already reaching some users running the latest versions of WhatsApp for iOS and Android.

WhatsApp doubled its group size limit from 512 to 1,024 members in November 2022, alongside the global rollout of Communities and its in-chat polls feature.

entry.title: Apple Watch Series 12 & Ultra 4 guide: Features, price and verdict
entry.content:
Macworld

In September 2026 Apple unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, with both models focusing much more heavily on health monitoring, Apple Intelligence and battery efficiency than on physical redesigns. Series 12 remains Apple’s mainstream premium smartwatch, while Ultra 4 continues as the larger, tougher model aimed at endurance sports, outdoor activities and diving. Both Apple Watches went on sale on September 18.

The biggest upgrade shared by both watches is Apple’s all-new Health Sensing System, which combines redesigned optical and electrical heart sensors with larger, more power-efficient green LEDs. Apple says it provides the most accurate heart-rate sensing of any wearable it tested. Background heart-rate readings are now taken every five seconds, while HRV can be measured as often as every five minutes – 60 times and 24 times more frequently respectively than on Series 11.

That additional data powers another major addition: Readiness, which gives users a 0–10 score based on recent activity, sleep, vitals and recovery data, and updates during the day. Both watches also use Apple’s new S11 chip, which enables Siri AI and a collection of Audio Intelligence features including Sound Recognition, faster Shazam, Live Rewind and Siri Recap. Live Rewind and Siri Recap are available to test in the watchOS 27.3 developer and public betas, as long as you have a paired iPhone running the corresponding iOS 27.3 beta. Both initially support English only.

The most dramatic hardware improvement is reserved for the Ultra 4: Apple has increased its normal-use battery-life rating from 42 hours to 50 hours, Low Power Mode from 72 to 84 hours, and introduced workout modes capable of tracking for up to 45 hours. Series 12 remains rated at 24 hours, although our testing found inconsistent battery life and charging performance, while the aluminium Series 12 gains tougher Ceramic Shield 2 and Apple has brought back a premium ceramic Apple Watch for the first time in years.

The five biggest Apple Watch upgrades for 2026

  1. New Health Sensing System with substantially more frequent heart-rate and HRV monitoring.
  2. Readiness score for daily recovery and training guidance.
  3. S11 chip, Siri AI and Audio Intelligence, including Siri Recap and Live Rewind, now in watchOS 27.3 beta testing.
  4. Much longer Ultra 4 battery life, rising from 42 to 50 hours, with up to 45 hours of extended workout tracking.
  5. New materials and durability, including Ceramic Shield 2 on aluminium Series 12 and the return of ceramic Series 12 models.

The rumours were broadly right that this wouldn’t be a major redesign, and also correctly predicted the emphasis on health, Siri AI and ceramic materials. However, rumours of Touch ID have not materialised, there is still no blood-glucose sensor, and the Series 12 hasn’t gained longer quoted battery life despite speculation about a larger battery. Starting prices are unchanged, although the 46mm Series 12 costs more.

Apple

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4: Specs compared

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 release date and availability

Apple announced the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 on September 9, 2026. Both models went on sale on September 18 and are available from Apple, authorized retailers and participating carriers.

watchOS 27 was released on September 14 for compatible existing Apple Watches.

Both watches are available now, including in the U.S., U.K., Australia, Canada and more than 50 other countries and regions.

You can buy them directly from Apple through Apple.com, the Apple Store app and Apple retail stores. They are also available through Apple-authorised retailers and, in the case of cellular models, participating mobile networks.

We recommend: Apple Watch Series 12 (42mm)

Price When Reviewed: $399
Best Prices Today: $329 at Amazon | $329 at Best Buy US | $389.99 at Walmart

We recommend: Apple Watch Ultra 4

Price When Reviewed: $799
Best Prices Today: $774 at Amazon | $774 at Walmart | $799 at Apple United States

Buy Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 at Apple U.S.

Buy Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 at Apple U.K.

Apple Watch Series 12 design

David Price / Foundry

The Series 12 does not represent a major external redesign, as the pre-launch rumours suggested. It retains Apple’s familiar rounded-square design and comes in 42mm and 46mm sizes.

Interestingly, the aluminium and titanium cases are fractionally wider than Series 11. The 46mm model measures 46 x 40 x 9.7mm, compared with 46 x 39 x 9.7mm for Series 11. The 42mm version measures 42 x 37 x 9.7mm, compared with 42 x 36 x 9.7mm previously. The screen resolutions remain 416×496 pixels and 374×446 pixels respectively.

Apple continues to offer aluminium and titanium models, but ceramic has returned as a premium case option. Ceramic models are fractionally larger and thicker, measuring 43mm or 47mm tall and 9.85mm thick.

The finishes are:

  • Aluminium: Dark Bronze, Light Gold, Black and Space Grey
  • Titanium: Radiant Gold and Natural
  • Ceramic: Pearl White and Night Blue

The ceramic options confirm one of the more interesting pre-launch rumours, although Apple opted for Night Blue rather than the dark grey that had also been indicated.

The Series 12 display remains a wide-angle LTPO3 Always-On Retina OLED with up to 2,000 nits brightness. Aluminium models now use Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple says is 60 percent tougher than the Ion-X glass used on Series 11. Titanium and ceramic versions use sapphire crystal.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 design

Apple

The Ultra 4 changes even less externally. It remains a 49mm Grade 5 titanium watch, measuring exactly 49 x 44 x 12mm, with the same 422×514-pixel display and 1,245 sq mm display area as Ultra 3.

It comes in the familiar Natural Titanium and Black Titanium finishes and retains its flat sapphire crystal display, raised protective case edges, prominent Digital Crown and orange-accented Action button.

The Ultra 4 is slightly heavier, however: 63.0g in Natural and 63.1g in Black, compared with 61.6g and 61.8g respectively for Ultra 3.

The display remains a wide-angle LTPO3 Always-On Retina display capable of 3,000 nits, so there is no headline screen-brightness upgrade.

Apple hasn’t introduced the rumoured Touch ID fingerprint sensor on the 2026 Apple Watch models. 

What about the buttons and controls?

Apple

The physical control layout is essentially unchanged.

Series 12 has:

  • Digital Crown with haptic feedback
  • Side button
  • Strap-release buttons

Ultra 4 adds the familiar:

  • Customisable Action button
  • Larger protected Digital Crown
  • Side button

The Action button can start workouts, mark segments, move to the next interval, activate the torch and perform other user-selected actions.

There is, however, a new single-tap finger-and-thumb gesture in addition to Double Tap and Wrist Flick, providing another way to interact without touching the display.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 health features

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 share the same new Health Sensing System and Readiness features. Paying more for the Ultra doesn’t get you more advanced core health sensors.

Mahmoud Itani / Foundry

More frequent heart-rate and HRV tracking

Both watches have redesigned optical and electrical heart sensors, including larger, more power-efficient green LEDs. Background heart-rate readings are taken every five seconds, while heart rate variability (HRV) can be measured as often as every five minutes. These more frequent measurements provide a fuller picture of your activity and recovery throughout the day.

The improvement is particularly significant for background monitoring. In Macwelt’s testing, Apple Watch Series 11 already recorded heart rate every five seconds during a workout, but its overnight readings were much less frequent and irregular. Across one sample night, the average interval was 4 minutes 39 seconds. Series 12’s five-second background readings therefore provide a denser record between workouts.

HRV measures variation in the time between heartbeats. The watches distinguish between Recovery HRV, which helps assess shorter-term stress and recovery, and overall HRV, which provides insight into longer-term health trends. Recovery HRV is also included in overnight Vitals, where it is compared with your personal baseline. A new daytime Vitals view shows heart rate and HRV, helping you spot changes outside your usual ranges.

Readiness: Should you push harder or take it easy?

Readiness combines recent activity, training load, daytime and overnight vitals, and sleep data into a score from 0 to 10. It provides one of four recommendations:

  • Recover: 0–1
  • Pace Yourself: 2–4
  • Ready: 5–7
  • Go For It: 8–10

The score updates throughout the day as you exercise, rest or take a nap. Open the Readiness app to see how activity, vitals and sleep are influencing it.

You’ll need to set up Activity, Sleep and overnight Vitals, enter your health details, and wear the watch to bed for at least seven nights before receiving a score. Readiness is a wellness guide: it doesn’t account for every medical condition or medication and shouldn’t be your sole basis for deciding whether it is safe to exercise.

Returning health features

Both watches retain ECG, high and low heart-rate notifications, irregular-rhythm notifications, blood oxygen tracking, sleep stages, sleep score, sleep apnea notifications and temperature-based Cycle Tracking. These features are also available on earlier compatible Apple Watches, although availability varies by model and region.

Hypertension notifications look for patterns associated with chronic high blood pressure over 30-day periods; they don’t provide a blood-pressure reading. The feature also supports earlier compatible models, and availability on Series 12 and Ultra 4 remains subject to regulatory clearance in some regions.

Do the new sensors affect battery life?

In Macwelt’s comparison of the Series 12 and Series 11, Halyna Kubiv recorded more background activity on the newer watch but lower energy consumption during the period after a hike.

That comparison covered a single day, and the watches differed in iPhone pairing and display use. It suggests the additional monitoring can be efficient, but doesn’t prove it has no effect on battery life.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 processor: What processor do they use?

Both watches use Apple’s new S11 chip, replacing the S10 used by Series 11 and Ultra 3.

Apple’s specifications list:

  • 64-bit dual-core processor
  • 4-core Neural Engine
  • 64GB storage
  • Secure hardware for Audio Intelligence processing

The S10 also had a 64-bit dual-core CPU, four-core Neural Engine and 64GB of storage, so the headline specifications alone don’t reveal how much faster S11 actually is. Apple calls it its “most powerful wearable chip”, but notably hasn’t provided a percentage CPU or GPU performance improvement over S10, and its technical specifications don’t list a separate GPU core count.

That means the more important S11 improvements appear to be what the chip enables rather than raw benchmark performance.

It works with the new Health Sensing System, supports Siri AI and powers the new Audio Intelligence functionality. Apple has also emphasised efficiency, particularly in relation to higher-frequency sensor readings and Ultra 4’s improved battery life.

The new Audio Intelligence system includes a Secure Exclave, a hardware-isolated area of the S11 that processes audio separately and deletes raw audio immediately after processing.

2026 Apple Watch connectivity

David Price / Foundry

Connectivity changes are modest. Cellular Series 12 and Ultra 4 models support 5G RedCap and LTE, as did their predecessors, with no newly branded Apple-designed modem.

Both watches also support Wi-Fi 4 (802.11n) on 2.4GHz and 5GHz, Bluetooth 5.3, and Apple’s second-generation Ultra Wideband chip. Wi-Fi 4 may sound dated, but Apple Watch relies mainly on Bluetooth and has relatively low data requirements.

Satellite connectivity

Satellite communications remain a major distinction between the Series and Ultra families.

Apple Watch Series 12 doesn’t have built-in satellite connectivity.

Ultra 4 does, supporting Emergency SOS via satellite and Find My location sharing via satellite when cellular and Wi-Fi aren’t available.

This is in addition to Messages via Satellite, which arrived in September 2025 with the Apple Watch Ultra 3. That feature lets you send and receive personal messages when your watch has no cellular or Wi-Fi coverage. However, Messages via satellite is available only in the US, Canada, Mexico and Japan. The new Emergency SOS via satellite is available in the U.S., Canada, U.K., Australia, New Zealand, various European countries, Japan and Mexico. No cellular plan is required for Emergency SOS via satellite.

This is broadly what had been expected before launch: Satellite remains primarily an Ultra feature rather than migrating to the regular Series watch.

2026 Apple Watch battery and charging: What’s new?

Apple

Apple Watch Series 12

Apple rates Series 12 for:

  • Up to 24 hours normal use
  • Up to 38 hours in Low Power Mode
  • Up to 10 hours of outdoor workout tracking

Those first two figures are unchanged from Series 11, so despite rumours that Apple was working on a larger battery, there is no increase in Apple’s quoted everyday battery life.

Apple claims improved endurance from a short charge.

Apple quotes the following charging figures for Series 12:

  • 80 percent in around 30 minutes
  • Up to 12 hours of use from a 15-minute charge
  • Up to 10 hours of sleep tracking from five minutes of charging

Apple also rated Series 11 for an 80 percent charge in around 30 minutes, and up to eight hours of normal use from a 15-minute charge.

In our Apple Watch Series 12 review, we recorded 51 and 40 hours of battery life across two runs – an average of 45.5 hours, compared with 47.5 hours for Series 11. Charging also varied: our watch reached 58% and 72% after 30 minutes in separate tests, falling short of Apple’s claimed 80%. These results show that the Series 12 can comfortably exceed Apple’s 24-hour rating, but they don’t demonstrate a consistent improvement over Series 11. Actual battery life depends on usage.

A separate investigation by Macwelt’s Halyna Kubiv compared Series 11 and Series 12 during a seven-hour hike and subsequent everyday use. After the workout, Series 12 recorded more background activity but consumed less energy during the measured period. However, this was a one-day comparison with different conditions: Series 11 was actively paired with an iPhone and handling notifications, while Series 12 was not, and display use differed.

Apple Watch Ultra 4

Battery life is one of Ultra 4’s biggest upgrades.

Apple rates it for:

  • 50 hours normal use, up from 42 hours
  • 84 hours Low Power Mode, up from 72 hours
  • 18 hours standard outdoor workout tracking
  • 25 hours Extended Workout
  • 45 hours Max Extended Workout

Apple says the Extended Workout figure represents a 25 percent increase over the previous generation.

Apple says Ultra 4 can reach 80 percent in around 45 minutes, but 15 minutes of charging now provides up to 18 hours of use, versus 12 hours on Ultra 3.

Apple also credits more efficient workout algorithms with helping deliver the longer endurance.

Apple Watch charging

Both models use Apple’s magnetic fast-charging system with the Apple Watch Magnetic Fast Charger to USB-C Cable.

There is no change to the basic magnetic charging system this year.

Gym Strength: Personalized workouts with Fitness+

Apple Fitness+ is testing a new Gym Strength feature in watchOS 27.3. It builds a strength-training plan around your available equipment, schedule and readiness, with guided workouts and adjustable weights and repetition counts.

Gym Strength requires an Apple Fitness+ subscription. During testing, your Apple Watch must run the watchOS 27.3 beta, and the iPhone or iPad you use with it must also run the corresponding 27.3 beta. It is a software and subscription feature, rather than an exclusive hardware upgrade for Series 12 or Ultra 4. 

Siri AI: Availability and requirements

Siri AI remains in beta, with availability depending on your language and region. The watchOS 27.2 update, released on October 26, adds French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish alongside English. Apple says Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish and Vietnamese will follow by the end of 2026.

Siri AI requires an Apple Intelligence-enabled device set to a supported language. It is currently unavailable on Apple Watch in the European Union and is not available to users under 13.

What is Audio Intelligence?

Audio Intelligence is Apple’s collection of sound-based AI features for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. These include recognizing important sounds, identifying music, displaying recently spoken words and summarizing conversations.

Sound Recognition and automatic Music Recognition with Shazam are already available. Live Rewind and Siri Recap entered developer-beta testing with watchOS 27.3 on November 3, 2026, followed by public-beta testing on November 5, so are likely to arrive with the full version of watchOS 27.3 later in 2026.

These two features require a supported iPhone 16 or newer, excluding iPhone 16e, with Apple Intelligence and Siri AI enabled. They initially support English only, are restricted to users aged 18 or older, and are unavailable in China and initially in the European Union. Sound Recognition and automatic Music Recognition support a wider range of iPhones and do not share these restrictions.

How well does Live Rewind work?

In Macworld’s hands-on testing of the watchOS 27.3 beta, David Price found Live Rewind useful for recovering speech he had missed, particularly when the speaker was nearby. Transcription was generally convincing, but unfamiliar names, technical terms and more distant conversations sometimes produced errors or missing sentences.

Double-pressing the Digital Crown retrieves speech from the immediately preceding 15 seconds, including any silence within that period. It doesn’t search back for the last 15 seconds of conversation, so you need to trigger it promptly. Closing the transcript discards it unless you explicitly save the text to the Siri app; the original audio isn’t saved.

The feature also depends on having your compatible iPhone nearby: processing takes place locally on that phone. Activation produces a visible animation and an audible alert, and transcripts don’t identify individual speakers.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 price

Apple has kept its entry prices unchanged in both the U.S. and U.K. – contrary to pre-event speculation that the Series 12 could increase in price.

Series 12 pricing varies considerably depending on case material. Aluminium is the entry-level option, while titanium costs more and the newly revived ceramic models occupy the premium end of the range.

Starting prices are unchanged, but the larger Series 12 costs more. The 46mm aluminum model starts at $449/£419 with GPS or $549/£519 with cellular—an increase of $20/£20 over the equivalent Series 11 models.

Should you buy Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4?

Apple

Apple Watch Series 12 is the best choice for most people. It offers essentially all of Apple’s important new features – including the new Health Sensing System, Readiness, frequent HRV measurements, Siri AI and Audio Intelligence – in a considerably smaller and cheaper watch. Live Rewind and Siri Recap currently require the watchOS 27.3 beta.

Live Rewind is a useful backup for missed speech, but our beta testing found limitations in transcription accuracy, range and its 15-second recall window.

However, our Series 12 review found inconsistent battery life and charging, along with occasional sluggishness. These observations may not reflect an established problem affecting every watch, but they temper our recommendation, particularly for owners of recent models considering an upgrade.

The strongest reason to choose Ultra 4 is battery life. Its increase in Apple’s rated battery life from 42 to 50 hours makes it much more practical for people who regularly spend more than a day away from a charger, while the new 25- and 45-hour extended workout modes make it substantially more appealing to runners, hikers, cyclists and endurance athletes.

Ultra 4 is also the better choice for outdoor adventurers because of its brighter 3,000-nit display, dual-frequency GPS, rugged titanium construction, Action button, 100m water resistance, recreational diving support and satellite communications. Series 12 is the better everyday watch: lighter, less bulky, available in two sizes and substantially cheaper.
